title: How drone field mapping works — from flight plan to field map
excerpt: A behind-the-scenes look at our UAV workflow: planning a flight, stitching multispectral imagery, and turning pixels into per-plot health maps.
body:
Every field map we deliver starts the same way: a drone, a flight plan, and about twenty minutes of flying. Here's what happens between take-off and the per-plot health map a farmer sees on their phone.

## Step 1 — Planning the flight

We draw the field boundary once, and the flight software generates a lawnmower pattern with enough image overlap (around 75%) for clean stitching. Altitude is a trade-off: fly higher and you cover more ground; fly lower and each pixel covers a smaller patch of crop.

## Step 2 — Capturing multispectral imagery

The camera doesn't just record what our eyes see. Alongside the regular color image, it captures **near-infrared** bands — and healthy vegetation reflects near-infrared light very strongly.

A stressed plant often looks perfectly green to a human days before symptoms show. In the near-infrared bands, that stress is already visible.

## Step 3 — From pixels to a health map

Back at the lab (or in the cloud), the hundreds of overlapping photos are stitched into a single orthomosaic. From the spectral bands we compute vegetation indices — NDVI is the most familiar — and aggregate them per plot.

## What the farmer receives

Not a giant image file: a simple map with plots colored green, yellow, or red, plus a short note on which plots are worth scouting first. The goal is a decision, not a dataset.
